claim: Click chemistry can be used to construct DNA templates for sgRNA expression.
source: Here, we successfully use click chemistry to construct DNA templates for sgRNA expression
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates successful construction of sgRNA templates using click chemistry, as shown in Figure 1B and described in the methods.

claim: sgRNA/dCas9 binding creates an environment that is permissive for transcription initiation/termination, thus generating novel sense and antisense transcripts.
source: Here, we successfully use click chemistry to construct DNA templates for sgRNA expression and show, rather than acting simply as a roadblock, sgRNA/dCas9 binding creates an environment that is permissive for transcription initiation/termination, thus generating novel sense and antisense transcripts.
evidence: The manuscript presents Northern blotting data showing novel transcripts generated at HMS2 locus upon CRISPRi intervention.

claim: At HMS2 in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, sgRNA/dCas9 targeting to the non-template strand for antisense transcription results in antisense transcription termination.
source: At HMS2 in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, sgRNA/dCas9 targeting to the non-template strand for antisense transcription results in antisense transcription termination, premature termination of a proportion of sense transcripts and initiation of a novel antisense transcript downstream of the sgRNA/dCas9-binding site.
evidence: Northern blotting data in Figure 2F,G shows reduction in SUT650 antisense transcript levels.

claim: At HMS2, sgRNA/dCas9 targeting causes premature termination of a proportion of sense transcripts.
source: At HMS2 in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, sgRNA/dCas9 targeting to the non-template strand for antisense transcription results in antisense transcription termination, premature termination of a proportion of sense transcripts and initiation of a novel antisense transcript downstream of the sgRNA/dCas9-binding site.
evidence: Northern blotting in Figure 3D,E shows a truncated HMS2 sense transcript (At) in addition to full-length transcript (A).

claim: At HMS2, sgRNA/dCas9 targeting initiates a novel antisense transcript downstream of the sgRNA/dCas9-binding site.
source: At HMS2 in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, sgRNA/dCas9 targeting to the non-template strand for antisense transcription results in antisense transcription termination, premature termination of a proportion of sense transcripts and initiation of a novel antisense transcript downstream of the sgRNA/dCas9-binding site.
evidence: Northern blotting in Figure 2F,H shows a new shorter antisense transcript (Bt) detected upon XRN1 deletion.

claim: CRISPRi is not strand-specific at all loci.
source: This redefinition of the transcriptional landscape by CRISPRi demonstrates that it is not strand-specific and highlights the controls and locus understanding required to properly interpret results from CRISPRi interventions.
evidence: Data at HMS2 shows effects on both sense and antisense transcripts despite targeting only the antisense non-template strand.

claim: CRISPRi redefines the transcriptional landscape at HMS2.
source: This redefinition of the transcriptional landscape by CRISPRi demonstrates that it is not strand-specific and highlights the controls and locus understanding required to properly interpret results from CRISPRi interventions.
evidence: Multiple novel transcripts are generated at HMS2 upon CRISPRi intervention as shown by Northern blotting.

claim: CRISPRi is proposed to act as a strand-specific roadblock to repress transcription in eukaryotic cells.
source: CRISPRi, an adapted CRISPR-Cas9 system, is proposed to act as a strand-specific roadblock to repress transcription in eukaryotic cells using guide RNAs (sgRNAs) to target catalytically inactive Cas9 (dCas9)
evidence: This is a statement of the prevailing understanding in the field, supported by citations.

claim: CRISPRi offers an alternative to genetic interventions for studying pervasive antisense transcription.
source: CRISPRi, an adapted CRISPR-Cas9 system, is proposed to act as a strand-specific roadblock to repress transcription in eukaryotic cells using guide RNAs (sgRNAs) to target catalytically inactive Cas9 (dCas9) and offers an alternative to genetic interventions for studying pervasive antisense transcription.
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for the study and represents the intended application of CRISPRi.

claim: Eukaryotic genomes are pervasively transcribed.
source: Eukaryotic genomes are pervasively transcribed but the effect of this inter- and intragenic transcription is not fully understood (Mellor et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The effect of pervasive inter- and intragenic transcription is not fully understood.
source: Eukaryotic genomes are pervasively transcribed but the effect of this inter- and intragenic transcription is not fully understood (Mellor et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Antisense transcription alters the chromatin in the vicinity of sense promoters.
source: Of particular interest is the function of antisense transcription, which alters the chromatin in the vicinity of sense promoters (Lavender et al., 2016; Murray et al., 2015; Pelechano and Steinmetz, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Antisense transcription is associated with repression, activation or no change in levels of the corresponding sense transcript.
source: Of particular interest is the function of antisense transcription, which alters the chromatin in the vicinity of sense promoters (Lavender et al., 2016; Murray et al., 2015; Pelechano and Steinmetz, 2013), and is associated with repression, activation or no change in levels of the corresponding sense transcript (Murray et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Discerning the mechanism by which antisense transcription functions in gene regulation is confounded by the difficulty in ablating antisense transcription without direct genetic intervention.
source: Discerning the mechanism by which antisense transcription functions in gene regulation is confounded by the difficulty in ablating antisense transcription without direct genetic intervention (Bassett et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a challenge in the field, supported by citation.

claim: CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) can circumvent issues of genetic intervention by avoiding the need to manipulate endogenous DNA sequences.
source: A new approach, CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) (Qi et al., 2013), can circumvent these issues by avoiding the need to manipulate endogenous DNA sequences.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of CRISPRi, with citation to the original CRISPRi paper.

claim: dCas9 is recruited by single base-pairing guide RNAs (sgRNAs) targeting the non-template (NT) DNA strand.
source: An endonucleolytically dead version of Cas9 (dCas9) is recruited by single base-pairing guide RNAs (sgRNAs) targeting the non-template (NT) DNA strand, where it blocks transcription strand-specifically at the loci tested (Lenstra et al., 2015; Qi et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of CRISPRi as established in previous studies.

claim: dCas9 blocks transcription strand-specifically at the loci tested.
source: An endonucleolytically dead version of Cas9 (dCas9) is recruited by single base-pairing guide RNAs (sgRNAs) targeting the non-template (NT) DNA strand, where it blocks transcription strand-specifically at the loci tested (Lenstra et al., 2015; Qi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is the established understanding from previous studies, which the current manuscript challenges.

claim: dCas9 fusion with transcriptional repressors or activators allows both negative and positive regulations of transcription, respectively.
source: In a further adaptation, dCas9 fusion with transcriptional repressors or activators allows both negative and positive regulations of transcription, respectively (Gilbert et al., 2013; Gilbert et al., 2014)
evidence: This describes an adaptation of CRISPRi supported by citations.

claim: When dCas9 is fused with transcriptional repressors or activators, the strand-specificity is lost.
source: In a further adaptation, dCas9 fusion with transcriptional repressors or activators allows both negative and positive regulations of transcription, respectively (Gilbert et al., 2013; Gilbert et al., 2014), but the strand-specificity is lost and thus is not suitable for strand-specific repression of antisense transcription.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the fusion approach, supported by citations.

claim: The sgRNA component of the CRISPRi system consists of a constant region (82 nt) that binds to dCas9 and a variable region (20 nt) that is responsible for targeting.
source: The sgRNA compenent of the CRISPRi system consists of two regions: a constant region (82 nt) that binds to dCas9 and a variable region (20 nt) that is responsible for targeting.
evidence: This describes the structure of sgRNAs as established knowledge.

claim: The modular nature of the sgRNA lends itself to production from DNA templates constructed using synthetic copper(I)-catalysed alkyne-azide cycloaddition (CuAAC) click chemistry.
source: The modular nature of the sgRNA lends itself to production from DNA templates constructed using synthetic copper(I)-catalysed alkyne-azide cycloaddition (CuAAC) click chemistry (El-Sagheer and Brown, 2010).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the modular structure, supported by citation to click chemistry methodology.

claim: The stable artificial triazole DNA linker generated by click chemistry is biocompatibile.
source: The stable artificial triazole DNA linker generated is biocompatibile, being read and accurately copied by DNA and RNA polymerases (Birts et al., 2014; El-Sagheer and Brown, 2011; El-Sagheer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work on click chemistry.

claim: The triazole DNA linker is read and accurately copied by DNA and RNA polymerases.
source: The stable artificial triazole DNA linker generated is biocompatibile, being read and accurately copied by DNA and RNA polymerases (Birts et al., 2014; El-Sagheer and Brown, 2011; El-Sagheer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Click chemistry is an efficient method for sgRNA template construction.
source: We show that click chemistry is an efficient method for sgRNA template construction
evidence: Figure 1B shows high efficiency of click reactions, and Figure 1C shows comparable PCR efficiencies.

claim: sgRNAs produced from click chemistry templates are as effective as sgRNAs produced from chemically synthesised full-length DNA templates at reducing levels of transcripts in vivo.
source: We show that click chemistry is an efficient method for sgRNA template construction and that when combined with dCas9, these sgRNAs are as effective as sgRNAs produced from chemically synthesised full-length DNA templates at reducing levels of transcripts in vivo.
evidence: Figure 2G shows comparable repression efficiency between clicked and full-length synthetic constructs.

claim: It is not completely understood how the CRISPRi system functions strand-specifically.
source: However, it is still not completely understood how the CRISPRi system functions strand-specifically or why sgRNAs must target the non-template strand.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: It is not understood why sgRNAs must target the non-template strand.
source: However, it is still not completely understood how the CRISPRi system functions strand-specifically or why sgRNAs must target the non-template strand.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: SUT650 represses HMS2 sense transcription.
source: We have previously used a promoter deletion of the antisense transcript SUT650 at the HMS2 locus to show that SUT650 represses HMS2 sense transcription (Nguyen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: PCR products from clicked templates were inserted in place of a URA3 selection cassette in the endogenous snR52 locus for expression of sgRNA.
source: The PCR products were inserted in place of a URA3 selection cassette in the endogenous snR52 locus for expression of a transcript that is then processed to form the mature nuclear-retained sgRNA (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Levels of dCas9 protein were uniform between strains.
source: Levels of dCas9 protein were uniform between strains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 shows uniform dCas9 expression.

claim: Insertion of URA3 into snR52 did not affect growth rate.
source: Neither insertion of URA3 into snR52 nor dCas9 expression in the control strains affected growth rate
evidence: This is stated based on growth rate measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: dCas9 expression in the control strains did not affect growth rate.
source: Neither insertion of URA3 into snR52 nor dCas9 expression in the control strains affected growth rate
evidence: This is stated based on growth rate measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Strains expressing some sgRNAs grew more slowly indicating a physiological effect.
source: Neither insertion of URA3 into snR52 nor dCas9 expression in the control strains affected growth rate, although strains expressing some sgRNAs grew more slowly indicating a physiological effect (Figure 1D).
evidence: Growth rate data in Figure 1D shows slower growth for some sgRNA-expressing strains.

claim: CRISPRi represses transcription when sgRNAs/dCas9 are targeted to the non-template (NT) strand next to a protospacer adjacent motif (PAM).
source: CRISPRi represses transcription when sgRNAs/dCas9 are targeted to the non-template (NT) strand next to a protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) (Qi et al., 2013) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: An engineered version of GAL1 has a stable antisense transcript (GAL1 AS) initiating within an ADH1 terminator inserted into the GAL1 coding region.
source: Firstly, we used an engineered version of GAL1 that has a stable antisense transcript (GAL1 AS) initiating within an ADH1 terminator inserted into the GAL1 coding region (Murray et al., 2012) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes the engineered locus used in the study, supported by citation and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: GAL1 AS is present in cells grown in glucose-containing media when the GAL1 gene is repressed.
source: GAL1 AS is present in cells grown in glucose-containing media when the GAL1 gene is repressed and is reduced as cells are switched into galactose-containing media and GAL1 sense is induced (Figure 2C lanes 1–3).
evidence: Northern blot data in Figure 2C shows GAL1 AS levels under different conditions.

claim: GAL1 AS is reduced as cells are switched into galactose-containing media and GAL1 sense is induced.
source: GAL1 AS is present in cells grown in glucose-containing media when the GAL1 gene is repressed and is reduced as cells are switched into galactose-containing media and GAL1 sense is induced (Figure 2C lanes 1–3).
evidence: Northern blot data in Figure 2C shows reduction of GAL1 AS upon galactose induction.

claim: Only sgRNA AS+112NT/dCas9 caused significant reduction in GAL1 antisense transcript levels.
source: Only sgRNA AS+112NT/dCas9 caused significant (p=0.004) reduction in GAL1 antisense transcript levels, as assessed by Northern blotting (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Northern blotting data in Figure 2C,D shows significant reduction only with AS+112NT.

claim: HMS2 has a stable antisense transcript, SUT650, initiating within the 3' coding region of HMS2.
source: Next, we examined the HMS2 locus which has a stable antisense transcript, SUT650, initiating within the 3' coding region of HMS2 (Nguyen et al., 2014; Pelechano et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous characterization of the locus.

claim: There is considerable heterogeneity in the SUT650 TSS.
source: Note that there is considerable heterogeneity in the SUT650 TSS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: TIF-seq data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 shows multiple TSS positions for SUT650.

claim: sgRNA AS+59NT may be binding upstream of the SUT650 TSS in some cells.
source: Note that there is considerable heterogeneity in the SUT650 TSS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and thus in some cells, sgRNA AS+59NT may be binding upstream of the SUT650 TSS.
evidence: This is inferred from the heterogeneity of TSS shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: AS+243NT/dCas9 significantly reduced SUT650.
source: AS+243NT/dCas9 significantly (p=0.011) reduced SUT650 (Figure 2F lanes 1 and 3, 2G)
evidence: Northern blotting data in Figure 2F,G shows significant reduction of SUT650.

claim: Repression of SUT650 by AS+243NT/dCas9 was comparable for the clicked and control full-length synthetic constructs.
source: AS+243NT/dCas9 significantly (p=0.011) reduced SUT650 (Figure 2F lanes 1 and 3, 2G) and this repression was comparable for the clicked and control full-length synthetic constructs (Figure 2G).
evidence: Quantification in Figure 2G shows similar repression levels for both construct types.

claim: There was no obvious effect of sgRNAs AS+59NT and AS+276NT on SUT650 levels.
source: However, there was no obvious effect of the other two sgRNAs/dCas9 on SUT650 levels (Figure 2F lanes 1, 4 and 5, 2G).
evidence: Northern blotting data in Figure 2F,G shows no change in SUT650 levels with these sgRNAs.

claim: dCas9 binding could only be detected at the site of sgRNA AS+243NT binding and not to the other two SUT650-targeting sgRNA binding sites tested.
source: Consistently, we could only detect dCas9 binding to the site of sgRNA AS+243NT binding and not to the other two SUT650-targeting sgRNA binding sites tested (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: ChIP data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 shows dCas9 enrichment only at AS+243NT site.

claim: CRISPR efficiency has been linked to nucleosome occupancy.
source: CRISPR efficiency has been linked to nucleosome occupancy (Horlbeck et al., 2016b; Isaac et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There was no correlation between the level of repression and the nucleosome occupancy at each of the SUT650 sgRNA target regions.
source: CRISPR efficiency has been linked to nucleosome occupancy (Horlbeck et al., 2016b; Isaac et al., 2016), but we found no correlation between the level of repression and the nucleosome occupancy (Knight et al., 2014) at each of the SUT650 sgRNA target regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Comparison of repression data with nucleosome occupancy data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 shows no correlation.

claim: Factors such as sequence determinants can influence CRISPRi repression.
source: However, other factors such as sequence determinants can also influence repression (Horlbeck et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: CRISPRi is suitable for reducing levels of antisense transcripts in yeast.
source: These results at GAL1 and HMS2 confirm CRISPRi is suitable for reducing levels of antisense transcripts in yeast
evidence: This is concluded from the successful repression observed at both loci.

claim: Controls are needed for each sgRNA designed to ensure that repression has been achieved.
source: These results at GAL1 and HMS2 confirm CRISPRi is suitable for reducing levels of antisense transcripts in yeast but controls are needed for each sgRNA designed to ensure that repression has been achieved.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that not all designed sgRNAs were effective.

claim: SUT650 is a substrate for the major cytoplasmic 5'−3' exonuclease Xrn1.
source: Since SUT650 is a substrate for the major cytoplasmic 5'−3' exonuclease Xrn1 (Figure 2F, lanes 1 and 2)
evidence: Northern blot data in Figure 2F shows stabilization of SUT650 upon XRN1 deletion.

claim: SUT650 was not stabilised upon XRN1 deletion in the strain expressing AS+243NT/dCas9.
source: Whilst SUT650 was not stabilised upon XRN1 deletion in the strain expressing AS+243NT/dCas9, supporting previous studies that CRISPRi operates via a transcriptional block (Qi et al., 2013) (Figure 2F, lanes 3 and 6, transcript B)
evidence: Northern blot data in Figure 2F shows no stabilization of SUT650 in the CRISPRi strain upon XRN1 deletion.

claim: CRISPRi operates via a transcriptional block.
source: Whilst SUT650 was not stabilised upon XRN1 deletion in the strain expressing AS+243NT/dCas9, supporting previous studies that CRISPRi operates via a transcriptional block (Qi et al., 2013) (Figure 2F, lanes 3 and 6, transcript B)
evidence: The lack of stabilization upon XRN1 deletion supports transcriptional rather than post-transcriptional mechanism, consistent with previous studies.

claim: A shorter antisense transcript (Bt) was detected upon XRN1 deletion in the strain expressing AS+243NT/dCas9.
source: Whilst SUT650 was not stabilised upon XRN1 deletion in the strain expressing AS+243NT/dCas9, supporting previous studies that CRISPRi operates via a transcriptional block (Qi et al., 2013) (Figure 2F, lanes 3 and 6, transcript B), we detected a shorter antisense transcript (Figure 2F, lane 6, transcript Bt).
evidence: Northern blot in Figure 2F shows a shorter transcript Bt in lane 6.

claim: Antisense transcript Bt extends into the HMS2 sense promoter.
source: With antisense-specific probes H1 and H2 in the HMS2 gene promoter and 5' coding region, respectively, we could detect antisense transcript Bt, indicating that it extends into the HMS2 sense promoter.
evidence: Northern blotting with multiple probes in Figure 2H shows Bt is detected by probes H1 and H2.

claim: Transcript Bt initiates upstream of the H4 probe site at the 3' end of the HMS2 gene.
source: However, probe H4 at the 3' end of the HMS2 gene was unable to hybridise to Bt, indicating that Bt initiates upstream of this site.
evidence: Northern blotting in Figure 2H shows Bt is not detected by probe H4.

claim: CRISPRi successfully blocked the original SUT650.
source: So whilst CRISPRi successfully blocked the original SUT650, a new Xrn1-sensitive unstable antisense transcript (Bt) was created.
evidence: Northern blotting data shows reduction of SUT650 and appearance of new transcript Bt.

claim: A new Xrn1-sensitive unstable antisense transcript (Bt) was created by CRISPRi.
source: So whilst CRISPRi successfully blocked the original SUT650, a new Xrn1-sensitive unstable antisense transcript (Bt) was created.
evidence: Northern blotting shows Bt is only detected upon XRN1 deletion, indicating it is Xrn1-sensitive.

claim: The new antisense transcript Bt is potentially due to changes in the chromatin structure caused by AS+243NT/dCas9 binding.
source: This is potentially due to changes in the chromatin structure caused by AS+243NT/dCas9 binding to this region (Horlbeck et al., 2016b; Isaac et al., 2016)
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations to studies on chromatin effects of CRISPR.

claim: The new antisense transcript Bt is potentially due to blocking SUT650, creating an environment that is permissive for transcription initiation.
source: This is potentially due to changes in the chromatin structure caused by AS+243NT/dCas9 binding to this region (Horlbeck et al., 2016b; Isaac et al., 2016) or by blocking SUT650, creating an environment that is permissive for transcription initiation (Murray et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation to previous work on transcription initiation.

claim: GAL1 AS repression by AS+112NT/dCas9 did not affect the GAL1 sense transcript levels.
source: Using CRISPRi, we also observed no significant change in GAL1 sense transcript levels or size (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Northern blotting data in Figure 3A,B shows no change in GAL1 sense levels.

claim: GAL1 AS repression by AS+112NT/dCas9 did not affect the GAL1 sense transcript size.
source: Using CRISPRi, we also observed no significant change in GAL1 sense transcript levels or size (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Northern blotting data in Figure 3A,B shows no change in GAL1 sense transcript size.

claim: Mutation of a TATA-like sequence ablated antisense transcription at GAL1 but observed no difference in GAL1 sense transcript levels.
source: Previously we mutated a TATA-like sequence to ablate antisense transcription but observed no difference in GAL1 sense transcript levels in the population under repressive or activating conditions (Murray et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: There was no leaky expression of the GAL1 sense transcript under repressive conditions (glucose) when the GAL1 AS transcript was blocked.
source: Additionally, we observed no leaky expression of the GAL1 sense transcript under repressive conditions (glucose) when the GAL1 AS transcript was blocked (Figure 3A, t = 0).
evidence: Northern blot data in Figure 3A shows no GAL1 sense expression at t=0 in glucose.

claim: GAL1 sense transcript polyA site usage was unaffected by sgRNA AS+112NT/dCas9.
source: To support a strand-specific transcriptional block of antisense transcription, GAL1 sense transcript polyA site usage was unaffected by sgRNA AS+112NT/dCas9 (Figure 3C).
evidence: 3' RACE data in Figure 3C shows same polyA sites in control and AS+112NT strains.

claim: XRN1 deletion in the GAL1 AS+112NT strain did not affect polyA site usage.
source: Furthermore, XRN1 deletion in this strain also did not affect polyA site usage, ruling out a partial double-stranded transcriptional block and subsequent destabilisation of the resulting truncated sense transcript (Figure 3C).
evidence: 3' RACE data in Figure 3C shows same polyA sites with and without XRN1.

claim: Reducing SUT650 transcription increases HMS2 sense transcript levels.
source: Previous work shows that reducing SUT650 transcription increases HMS2 sense transcript levels (Nguyen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: A considerably shortened HMS2 sense transcript (At) was detected in addition to the full-length HMS2 sense transcript (A) in the AS+243NT/dCas9 strain.
source: To our surprise, in addition to the full-length HMS2 sense transcript (A), we detected a considerably shortened HMS2 sense transcript (At).
evidence: Northern blotting in Figure 3D shows both A and At transcripts.

claim: The combined levels of the truncated and full-length HMS2 sense transcripts are similar to those in the strain not expressing an sgRNA, independent of the presence of XRN1.
source: Since the combined levels of the truncated and full-length transcripts are similar to those in the strain not expressing an sgRNA, independent of the presence of XRN1 (Figure 3D, lanes 1 and 3 or 2 and 6)
evidence: Northern blotting data in Figure 3D shows similar total HMS2 sense levels.

claim: The AS+243NT/dCas9 complex bound within the HMS2 coding region may be causing partial premature sense transcription termination.
source: Since the combined levels of the truncated and full-length transcripts are similar to those in the strain not expressing an sgRNA, independent of the presence of XRN1 (Figure 3D, lanes 1 and 3 or 2 and 6), we hypothesised that the AS+243NT/dCas9 complex bound within the HMS2 coding region may be causing partial premature sense transcription termination, leading to transcript At.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation of truncated transcript At.

claim: Both transcripts A and At could be detected using probes upstream of the AS+243NT/dCas9 binding site.
source: Both transcripts A and At could clearly be detected using the probes upstream of the AS+243NT/dCas9 binding site (probes H1, H2, H3)
evidence: Northern blotting with multiple probes in Figure 3E shows detection of both A and At with upstream probes.

claim: The truncated HMS2 sense transcript At was undetectable using probe H4 downstream of the AS+243NT/dCas9 binding site.
source: Both transcripts A and At could clearly be detected using the probes upstream of the AS+243NT/dCas9 binding site (probes H1, H2, H3), but the truncated transcript was undetectable using probe H4 downstream of this site.
evidence: Northern blotting in Figure 3E shows At is not detected by probe H4.

claim: The transcriptional block caused by AS+243NT/dCas9 is not strand-specific.
source: Thus, the transcriptional block caused by AS+243NT/dCas9 is not strand-specific and re-defines the transcriptional landscape at the HMS2 locus by creating a chromatin environment that is suitable for both transcription initiation and termination.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation of effects on both sense and antisense transcripts.

claim: AS+243NT/dCas9 re-defines the transcriptional landscape at the HMS2 locus by creating a chromatin environment that is suitable for both transcription initiation and termination.
source: Thus, the transcriptional block caused by AS+243NT/dCas9 is not strand-specific and re-defines the transcriptional landscape at the HMS2 locus by creating a chromatin environment that is suitable for both transcription initiation and termination.
evidence: This is inferred from the generation of novel transcripts with new initiation and termination sites.

claim: Three sgRNAs designed to bind the non-template strand adjacent to PAM sites near the HMS2 sense TSS gave no CRISPRi repression.
source: To see if we could more directly target and block HMS2 sense transcripts, we designed three sgRNAs to bind the non-template strand adjacent to PAM sites near the HMS2 sense TSS (S+77NT, S+106NT, S+179NT) and monitored their effects on both HMS2 sense and antisense transcripts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). However, these sgRNAs gave no CRISPRi repression as indicated by the unchanged transcript levels and integrity.
evidence: Northern blotting data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 shows no change in transcript levels.

claim: Mutation of a TATA-like sequence within the ADH1 terminator greatly reduced the level of the GAL1 antisense transcript.
source: At GAL1, mutation of a TATA-like sequence within the ADH1 terminator greatly reduced the level of the GAL1 antisense transcript (Figure 4A,B) (Murray et al., 2015).
evidence: Northern blotting data in Figure 4B shows reduced GAL1 AS in TATA mutant, supported by citation.

claim: XRN1 deletion in the TATA mutant strain only slightly increased GAL1 AS levels, suggesting that most repression was at the level of transcription rather than altering transcript stability.
source: Since XRN1 deletion in the TATA mutant strain only slightly increased GAL1 AS levels, this suggests that most repression was at the level of transcription rather than altering transcript stability (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: Northern blotting data in Figure 4B,C shows minimal stabilization upon XRN1 deletion in TATA mutant.

claim: XRN1 deletion in the strain expressing AS+112NT/dCas9 resulted in some upregulation of GAL1 AS, indicating that antisense transcript repression was not as great in this strain.
source: By contrast, XRN1 deletion in the strain expressing AS+112NT/dCas9 did result in some upregulation of GAL1 AS (Figure 4B,C), indicating that antisense transcript repression was not as great in this strain.
evidence: Northern blotting data in Figure 4B,C shows stabilization of GAL1 AS upon XRN1 deletion in CRISPRi strain.

claim: The stabilised GAL1 AS transcript in the AS+112NT/dCas9 xrn1Δ strain was the same size as in the control.
source: Unlike at HMS2 (Figure 2F,G), this stabilised GAL1 AS transcript was the same size as in the control and so likely represents stabilisation of the transcripts escaping repression rather than novel transcripts.
evidence: Northern blotting in Figure 4B shows GAL1 AS is same size in all conditions.

claim: Replacement of the entire HMS2 coding region with URA3 successfully blocked SUT650 transcription and increased levels of the HMS2 sense transcript.
source: This successful block of SUT650 transcription increased levels of the HMS2 sense transcript, the di-cistronic HMS2-BAT2 transcript and consequently decreased levels of the downstream gene, BAT2, due to transcriptional interference (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: Northern blotting data in Figure 4F shows these effects in the HMS2:URA3 strain, supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Replacement of HMS2 coding region with URA3 increased levels of the di-cistronic HMS2-BAT2 transcript.
source: This successful block of SUT650 transcription increased levels of the HMS2 sense transcript, the di-cistronic HMS2-BAT2 transcript and consequently decreased levels of the downstream gene, BAT2, due to transcriptional interference (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: Northern blotting data in Figure 4F shows increased HMS2-BAT2 transcript.

claim: Replacement of HMS2 coding region with URA3 decreased levels of the downstream gene, BAT2, due to transcriptional interference.
source: This successful block of SUT650 transcription increased levels of the HMS2 sense transcript, the di-cistronic HMS2-BAT2 transcript and consequently decreased levels of the downstream gene, BAT2, due to transcriptional interference (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: Northern blotting data in Figure 4F shows decreased BAT2 transcript.

claim: CRISPRi resulted in a similar decrease in SUT650 as HMS2:URA3.
source: Whilst CRISPRi resulted in a similar decrease in SUT650 as HMS2:URA3, neither the HMS2, BAT2 nor HMS2-BAT2 di-cistronic transcripts were altered (Figure 4F).
evidence: Northern blotting data in Figure 4F shows comparable SUT650 reduction.

claim: CRISPRi did not alter HMS2, BAT2 or HMS2-BAT2 di-cistronic transcript levels.
source: Whilst CRISPRi resulted in a similar decrease in SUT650 as HMS2:URA3, neither the HMS2, BAT2 nor HMS2-BAT2 di-cistronic transcripts were altered (Figure 4F).
evidence: Northern blotting data in Figure 4F shows no change in these transcripts with CRISPRi.

claim: The discovery that AS+243NT/dCas9 represses SUT650, induces a new unstable HMS2 antisense transcript and prematurely terminates the sense transcript could explain why blocking SUT650 using CRISPRi and the URA3 gene body replacement strategies did not give the same results.
source: The discovery that whilst AS+243NT/dCas9 represses SUT650, a new unstable HMS2 antisense transcript is induced and the sense transcript is prematurely terminated could explain why blocking SUT650 using CRISPRi and the URA3 gene body replacement strategies did not give the same results (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the different transcriptional outcomes observed with the two methods.

claim: CRISPRi is not as effective as a genetic mutation in reducing levels of either the GAL1 or HMS2 AS transcripts.
source: Thus, CRISPRi is not as effective as a genetic mutation in reducing levels of either the GAL1 or HMS2 AS transcripts.
evidence: This is concluded from comparison of CRISPRi with genetic interventions at both loci.

claim: CRISPRi has been used to strand-specifically repress antisense transcription at GAL10.
source: Although CRISPRi has been used to strand-specifically repress antisense transcription at GAL10 (Lenstra et al., 2015) and GAL1 (this work)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: CRISPRi strand-specifically represses antisense transcription at GAL1.
source: Although CRISPRi has been used to strand-specifically repress antisense transcription at GAL10 (Lenstra et al., 2015) and GAL1 (this work)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in the current manuscript showing no effect on GAL1 sense transcript.

claim: CRISPRi is not strand-specific at HMS2.
source: Although CRISPRi has been used to strand-specifically repress antisense transcription at GAL10 (Lenstra et al., 2015) and GAL1 (this work), here we demonstrate that this is not true at HMS2.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the effects on both sense and antisense transcripts at HMS2.

claim: The lack of strand-specificity at HMS2 may reflect the vastly different transcription levels for the galactose-inducible genes (high) compared to HMS2 (low).
source: This may reflect the vastly different transcription levels for the galactose-inducible genes (high) compared to HMS2 (low).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the different outcomes at different loci.

claim: A study in human K562 cells found that CRISPRi-induced repression did not correlate with which strand was targeted at 49 genes.
source: Furthermore, a study in human K562 cells found that CRISPRi-induced repression did not correlate with which strand was targeted at 49 genes, although the mechanism behind this observation was not investigated (Gilbert et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work in human cells.

claim: The binding of the sgRNA/dCas9 complex at HMS2 creates a new chromatin environment which is permissible for transcription initiation and termination.
source: This work extends our previous hypothesis (Nguyen et al., 2014), allowing us to propose that, rather than acting as a roadblock, the binding of the sgRNA/dCas9 complex at HMS2 creates a new chromatin environment, either directly or indirectly via the blocking of antisense transcription, which is permissible for transcription initiation and termination.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation of novel transcripts with new initiation and termination sites.

claim: New transcription units are generated by CRISPRi that result in novel sense and antisense transcripts of varying stabilities.
source: This work extends our previous hypothesis (Nguyen et al., 2014), allowing us to propose that, rather than acting as a roadblock, the binding of the sgRNA/dCas9 complex at HMS2 creates a new chromatin environment, either directly or indirectly via the blocking of antisense transcription, which is permissible for transcription initiation and termination. Thus, new transcription units are generated that result in novel sense and antisense transcripts of varying stabilities that are therefore not always detectable.
evidence: This is concluded from the detection of novel transcripts with different stabilities (some only visible upon XRN1 deletion).

claim: Novel transcripts generated by CRISPRi are not always detectable due to varying stabilities.
source: Thus, new transcription units are generated that result in novel sense and antisense transcripts of varying stabilities that are therefore not always detectable.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some transcripts are only detected upon XRN1 deletion.

claim: The redefinition of the transcriptional landscape by CRISPRi highlights the levels of controls and locus understanding needed before results from using CRISPRi can be interpreted.
source: This redefinition of the transcriptional landscape highlights the levels of controls and locus understanding needed before results from using CRISPRi can be interpreted.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the unexpected effects observed at HMS2.

claim: Routine use of CRISPRi for gene expression analysis will require rigorous analysis of transcript integrity and function before conclusions can be drawn.
source: This suggests that routine use of CRISPRi for gene expression analysis will require rigorous analysis of transcript integrity and function before conclusions can be drawn.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study.

claim: PCR products from clicked templates had no significantly different efficiencies when compared to control full-length synthesised oligonucleotides.
source: A small library of single-stranded DNAs, comprised of templates for sgRNA variable regions, were joined to the constant region using click chemistry (Figure 1B) and used successfully as templates for PCR, with no significantly different efficiencies when compared to control full-length synthesised oligonucleotides (Figure 1C).
evidence: qPCR efficiency data in Figure 1C shows no significant differences (p>0.05).

claim: The click reaction showed high efficiency for all the HMS2 constructs.
source: A polyacrylamide gel visualised by UV shadowing reveals a high efficiency of the click reaction for all the HMS2 constructs
evidence: Figure 1B shows strong bands for clicked products for all constructs.

claim: SUT650 has a major transcription start site at position 705,244 bp on Chromosome X.
source: Transcript start and end sites on the Crick strand of Chromosome X for SUT650 as mapped by Transcript Isoform Sequencing (TIF-seq) (Pelechano et al., 2013). The main SUT650 transcript start site at position 705,244 bp was used in the positioning of the HMS2 AS-targeting sgRNAs
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1 shows TIF-seq data with the major TSS indicated.

claim: The click linkage was designed between a dCpT dinucleotide within the Cas9 handle region to increase the efficiency of the click reaction.
source: To increase the efficiency of the click reaction, the click linkage was designed between a dCpT dinucleotide within the Cas9 handle region.
evidence: This is stated as a design choice in the methods section.

claim: SNR52 is a Pol III-transcribed C/D box small nucleolar RNA (snoRNA) gene.
source: SNR52 is a Pol III-transcribed C/D box small nucleolar RNA (snoRNA) gene and so does not undergo extensive post-transcriptional processing such as capping and polyadenylation, and transcripts from this locus are retained in the nucleus.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about the SNR52 locus.

claim: SNR52 transcripts do not undergo extensive post-transcriptional processing such as capping and polyadenylation.
source: SNR52 is a Pol III-transcribed C/D box small nucleolar RNA (snoRNA) gene and so does not undergo extensive post-transcriptional processing such as capping and polyadenylation, and transcripts from this locus are retained in the nucleus.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of Pol III-transcribed snoRNAs.

claim: Transcripts from the SNR52 locus are retained in the nucleus.
source: SNR52 is a Pol III-transcribed C/D box small nucleolar RNA (snoRNA) gene and so does not undergo extensive post-transcriptional processing such as capping and polyadenylation, and transcripts from this locus are retained in the nucleus.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of snoRNAs.

claim: The SNR52 locus contains a self-splicing site that produces a mature transcript without additional machinery.
source: Additionally, the locus contains a self-splicing site that produces a mature transcript without additional machinery, allowing precise production of a mature sgRNA without any unwanted extensions.
evidence: This is stated as a feature of the SNR52 locus that makes it suitable for sgRNA expression.

claim: The self-splicing site in SNR52 allows precise production of a mature sgRNA without any unwanted extensions.
source: Additionally, the locus contains a self-splicing site that produces a mature transcript without additional machinery, allowing precise production of a mature sgRNA without any unwanted extensions.
